metadata.title: The relationship between cultural capital and the students’ perception of feedback across 75 countries: Evidence from PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds and applies PISA’s complex sampling design in multilevel models. At the student level, the authors use a pure student weight derived from the combination of student and class weights (W_FSTUWT) divided by the final school weight, and they apply the pure school weight (W_SCHGRNRABWT) at the cluster level, following Rutkowski et al. (2010). The analytic sample is restricted to 75 countries with valid outcome information (PERFEED), excluding four countries with missing outcome values. All models are estimated in Mplus 8.4 and student-level predictors are group-mean centered at the school mean (Enders & Tofighi; Caro & Lenkeit), which affects interpretation of within-school associations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable PERFEED is a student-perceived feedback index derived from questionnaire items on the frequency of directive feedback in reading lessons, not a cognitive achievement score with PISA plausible values. Because the paper reports excluding four countries with missing outcome-variable information but does not describe an explicit missing-data procedure for individual-level missingness on predictors, the missing-data handling for the remaining analytic sample is not fully documented. This is a reporting gap for missing predictor values, even though the outcome-variable country exclusions are clearly stated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2018 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds and restricts the analysis to 75 participating countries/economies. Four countries (Canada, Cyprus, Lebanon, and Macedonia) are excluded because the latent outcome variable for feedback (PERFEED) had missing-value issues. The models are estimated separately for each country using multilevel random-intercept regression with students nested within schools, and the analytic sample corresponds to the country-specific student counts reported in Table 3 (N=schools, n=students). The paper does not provide a detailed individual-level missing-data rule for predictors beyond the country-level outcome exclusion.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (lower secondary; directive feedback perception; 75 countries)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel random-intercept regression coefficients reported in Table 3 across countries (no single global ML metric). Example extremes: HEDRES positive in all countries except Thailand (non-significant there); JOYREAD positive and significant in most countries (non-significant in Netherlands and Moscow region). Gender effect: boys perceive more feedback than girls in every country; lowest in Qatar (β=-0.030, p<0.05) and highest in USA (β=-0.274, p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged home educational resources, reading enjoyment, parental education, parents’ occupational status, and gender to model perceived feedback (PERFEED) in lower secondary reading classrooms across 75 countries, finding that home educational resources and reading enjoyment show positive associations with perceived feedback in essentially all countries (with limited non-significant exceptions). This indicates that students’ cultural capital—especially objectified and embodied forms—may be linked to how frequently teachers’ directive feedback is perceived, suggesting that feedback practices could be targeted to reduce cultural-capital-related perception gaps, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 student questionnaire data for 15-year-olds in reading classes across 75 countries/economies, modeling PERFEED (students’ perceived frequency of directive teacher feedback) with multilevel random-intercept regression (students nested within schools). It reports country-specific regression coefficients (Table 3) rather than a single predictive accuracy metric, showing a consistent positive pattern for home educational resources (HEDRES) and reading enjoyment (JOYREAD) on perceived feedback, with non-significant exceptions (e.g., Thailand for HEDRES; Netherlands and Moscow region for JOYREAD). Parental education (PARED) is significant in only six countries with mixed directions, while parents’ occupational status (HISEI) is significantly negative in 20 countries. Gender is consistently significant across all countries, with boys perceiving more feedback than girls. The analysis is cross-sectional and does not establish causality; additionally, missing-data handling for predictors at the individual level is not fully specified beyond excluding four countries with missing PERFEED.
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper is included in an ML-focused search, the reported methodology is multilevel regression (random-intercept models in Mplus) rather than machine-learning prediction/classification. Consequently, no ML algorithms, PV handling, or ML performance metrics (e.g., AUC/RMSE) are applicable, and the extraction leaves ml_techniques empty. The study’s outcomes are regression associations across countries, so the extraction treats it as an exploratory cross-sectional modeling paper rather than an ML predictive pipeline.
